title: Neolithic and Chalcolithic Anatolia
subtitle: 10,000–3,000 BC · Göbekli Tepe, Çatalhöyük and the First Palace at Arslantepe

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: No kings, only horizons — foothill villages, the Konya plain towns, the western farmers and the first palace at Arslantepe

entries.label: Hallan Çemi — a village of foragers
entries.hint: On the Batman river, hunter-gatherers lived year-round in a settlement of round semi-subterranean houses with communal buildings, stone bowls and abundant evidence of fishing and gathering. It is one of the oldest known permanent villages in the Near East, built by people who had not yet domesticated anything. Settling came first; farming followed.
entries.note: Michael Rosenberg and R. Redding, 'Hallan Çemi and early village organization in eastern Anatolia', in I. Kuijt (ed.), Life in Neolithic Farming Communities (2000).

entries.label: Çayönü — the long sequence of a foothill village
entries.hint: Excavated from 1964 by Robert Braidwood and Halet Çambel, Çayönü shows a village rebuilding itself across some 1,500 years, from round huts through a succession of rectangular building types to larger multi-roomed houses. Its cult buildings, copper beads and early managed animals make it a reference sequence for the whole of the Taurus foothills.
entries.note: R. J. Braidwood and H. Çambel, Çayönü excavation reports (1964–); M. Özdoğan and A. Erim-Özdoğan, Çayönü publications (1990s–).

entries.label: Nevalı Çori — a village with a cult building
entries.hint: On a tributary of the Euphrates, Nevalı Çori held long rectangular houses on stone footings and a sunken cult building with limestone T-pillars and carved human heads. It was excavated by Harald Hauptmann from 1983 to 1991 and then flooded by the Atatürk Dam reservoir, which makes the published record all that remains of it.
entries.note: Harald Hauptmann, Nevalı Çori excavation reports (1983–91); H. Hauptmann, 'Ein Kultgebäude in Nevalı Çori', in M. Frangipane et al. (eds), Between the Rivers and over the Mountains (1993).

entries.label: Aşıklı Höyük — the first village of the plateau
entries.hint: Beside the Melendiz river, below the volcanic Hasan Dağ, a settlement of packed mudbrick rooms grew over nearly a millennium, with little in the way of streets and with open courts between clusters of houses. Obsidian from the nearby volcanoes was its raw material and its currency. It is the oldest known farming-herding village in central Anatolia.
entries.note: Ufuk Esin and Savaş Harmankaya, 'Aşıklı', in M. Özdoğan and N. Başgelen (eds), Neolithic in Turkey (2007).

entries.label: Çatalhöyük East — a town without streets
entries.hint: Several thousand people lived at Çatalhöyük at its height — estimates run from a few thousand to around eight thousand — in mudbrick houses pressed wall to wall and entered through the roof. There were no streets and no public buildings. Excavated by James Mellaart in 1961–65 and by Ian Hodder's team from 1993 to 2018, it is the most closely studied Neolithic settlement in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012.
entries.note: James Mellaart, Çatal Hüyük: A Neolithic Town in Anatolia (1967); Ian Hodder, The Leopard's Tale (2006); UNESCO World Heritage List no. 1405.

entries.label: Çatalhöyük West — a new site, new houses, pottery
entries.hint: Around 6000 BC the people of the East Mound moved to a neighbouring mound to the west. The houses there are freestanding, with courtyards and fewer buried dead, and pottery in quantity appears at last. It is the same community, living differently, a few hundred metres away.
entries.note: Ian Hodder (ed.), Çatalhöyük Research Project volumes, esp. Çatalhöyük West Mound (2013 summary); Mellaart 1967.

entries.label: The Neolithic arrives on the Aegean shore
entries.hint: Around 6700 BC the first farming villages appear on the Aegean coast — at Çukuriçi Höyük beside Ephesus and at Ulucak near İzmir — and, shortly after, around the Sea of Marmara at Barcın and Menteşe. They had boats, cattle, sheep and the full package of crops, and they were the springboard of the farmers who then reached Greece and the Balkans.
entries.note: Barbara Horejs et al., 'The Aegean in the Early 7th Millennium BC: Maritime Networks and Colonization', Journal of World Prehistory 28 (2015); Ulucak Höyük excavation reports (Çevik, Çilingiroğlu).

entries.label: Hacılar — painted-pottery villages of the Lake District
entries.hint: Mellaart's digs at Hacılar (1957–60) revealed a village of rectangular mudbrick houses with plastered floors, a fine painted pottery and rows of clay figurines. It showed that central Anatolia was not alone: the Lakes District had its own early farming culture, with its own look, a few hundred kilometres from Çatalhöyük.
entries.note: James Mellaart, Excavations at Hacılar (1970).

entries.label: The Upper Euphrates chiefdoms
entries.hint: By the fourth millennium BC the settlements of the Malatya plain and the Euphrates bend — Arslantepe, Norşuntepe, Tepecik, Hacınebi — were becoming socially ranked. They had large public storehouses, differences in burial wealth and the first buildings that were more than houses. The people who built them have no name; the settlement hierarchy is what they have left.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane, 'Fourth millennium Arslantepe: the development of a centralised society without urbanisation', Origini 34 (2012); Gil Stein, Rethinking World-Systems (1999).

entries.label: Arslantepe VII — Temple C
entries.hint: In Period VII, a mudbrick temple with painted walls stood on a prepared platform, with a large hall and rooms where food was stored and shared. Whoever ran it controlled the surplus. The building is the architectural prelude to the palace that replaced it after about 3350 BC.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane (ed.), Arslantepe excavation volumes (Rome, 1993–); Frangipane 2012.

entries.label: Arslantepe VIA — the first known palace
entries.hint: Around 3350 BC a palace complex rose on the mound — a monumental courtyard, a hall with wall paintings, and a series of storerooms in which thousands of clay sealings were found. Residential, political, administrative and ceremonial functions sat in one compound. It is the oldest known palace in the Near East and it stood without a city around it.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane, 'Arslantepe, Malatya: A prehistoric and early historic centre', and the Arslantepe excavation series (1993–); Frangipane (ed.), Economic Centralisation in Formative States (2010).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Healed skulls at Çatalhöyük, a fortified citadel at Mersin and the burning of the Arslantepe palace

entries.label: Healed skulls at Çatalhöyük
entries.hint: A study of the town's skeletons found healed fractures in about a quarter of the 93 adult skulls examined, many from repeated blows to the head delivered from behind with hard, rounded objects — clay balls from the site are about the right size. Injuries peaked in the middle phase, when the town was largest. The 'peaceful town' of earlier accounts was not entirely so.
entries.note: Clark Spencer Larsen et al., 'Bioarchaeology of Neolithic Çatalhöyük reveals fundamental transitions in health, mobility, and lifestyle in early farmers', PNAS 116 (2019).

entries.label: The citadel of Mersin-Yumuktepe
entries.hint: In the Middle Chalcolithic, Level XVI at Yumuktepe on the Cilician coast was ringed by a massive stone-founded mudbrick wall with a gate, bastions and rows of narrow storage rooms, which John Garstang interpreted as a barracks citadel. More recent work argues the layout reflects social organisation rather than only defence, but it remains the earliest monumentally fortified settlement in Anatolia.
entries.note: John Garstang, Prehistoric Mersin (1953); Mara Palumbi and Isabella Caneva (eds), The Chalcolithic at Mersin-Yumuktepe: Level XVI Reconsidered (2019).

entries.label: The burning of the Arslantepe palace
entries.hint: Around 3000 BC the palace burned in a great fire that sealed thousands of objects — including swords and spearheads — beneath collapsed walls. Whether it was an internal revolt or an attack by outsiders is unresolved. What followed was not an abandonment: wattle-and-daub huts and Kura-Araxes-type pottery now stood on the same site.
entries.note: Frangipane 2010 and the Arslantepe series.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A society of houses, the first stamp seals, and a bureaucracy that kept its books in clay sealings

entries.label: A town of houses, not of institutions
entries.hint: Çatalhöyük's houses were all of similar size and layout, and none was obviously a palace or a temple. Individual houses were rebuilt on the same footprint over generations, with the dead buried under the floors — so that the house, with its ancestors beneath it, was the main unit of social memory and property. Hodder has argued that this produced a deliberately egalitarian town.
entries.note: Ian Hodder, The Leopard's Tale (2006); Hodder (ed.), Çatalhöyük Research Project volumes (2005–2014).

entries.label: Stamp seals and clay stamps
entries.hint: Carved clay and stone stamps appear in Neolithic Anatolia, with geometric and spiral designs, and were probably used for marking textiles, bread or the body, or to claim goods. They are the beginnings of a mark of ownership that would, in the Late Chalcolithic, become a means of securing storerooms and goods by sealing their closures.
entries.note: James Mellaart, Çatal Hüyük (1967); Çatalhöyük Research Project finds volumes (Hodder, ed.).

entries.label: Sealings and rations at Arslantepe
entries.hint: Thousands of clay sealings from the palace storerooms recorded who stored what and who authorised its release, with seal designs showing lions, snakes and human figures. Mass-produced bowls made in their thousands appear to have been issued as food rations. Writing never came, but a centralised system of control did; it is among the earliest documented bureaucracies in the world.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane (ed.), Arslantepe Cretulae: An Early Centralised Administrative System Before Writing (2007); Frangipane (ed.) 2010.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The first monumental sanctuaries, the skull building, painted houses and burials beneath the floor

entries.label: Göbekli Tepe — the first monumental sanctuary
entries.hint: On a limestone ridge above the Harran plain, people with no farming, no pottery and no metals set up circular enclosures of T-shaped limestone pillars up to about five metres high, many carved with foxes, boars, snakes and birds. It was built by hunter-gatherers, probably gathering at intervals for communal feasting and ritual, and it pushes monumental architecture back by some 6,000 years. UNESCO inscribed it in 2018.
entries.note: Klaus Schmidt, Göbekli Tepe: A Stone Age Sanctuary in South-Eastern Anatolia (2012); Oliver Dietrich et al., Antiquity 86 (2012); UNESCO World Heritage List no. 1572.

entries.label: Karahan Tepe and the Stone Hills
entries.hint: Göbekli Tepe turned out not to be alone. At Karahan Tepe, a sunken rock-cut chamber with T-pillars and rows of carved figures was found from 2019 on, and a dozen related sites now make up the 'Taş Tepeler' (Stone Hills) region. These findings are preliminary, and interpretations are still being formed.
entries.note: Karahan Tepe excavation reports (Necmi Karul, Istanbul University), 2019–; Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism's Taş Tepeler project, 2020–. Preliminary as of 2026.

entries.label: The Skull Building at Çayönü
entries.hint: A rectangular building beside the village held the bone fragments of several hundred people, with skulls stacked in the cellars and a flat slab nearby in which blood residues of humans and animals were reported. It is read as a place where the dead were kept and processed, rather than a record of massacre; some of its interpretations, notably the sacrificial-altar reading, remain contested.
entries.note: Mehmet Özdoğan and Aslı Erim-Özdoğan, Çayönü reports; W. Loy and A. Wood, Journal of Field Archaeology 16 (1989) on the blood residues; the Bordeaux thesis on the Skull Building human remains (2010).

entries.label: Painted walls and bulls' horns at Çatalhöyük
entries.hint: Rooms with plastered bull horns, painted vultures, a hunting scene around an aurochs and sets of cattle skulls set in benches were taken by Mellaart as shrines to a mother goddess. Hodder's team found that the same imagery appears in ordinary houses, that there is no clean divide between a shrine and a home, and that the 'goddess' reading rests on a handful of finds.
entries.note: Mellaart 1967; Ian Hodder, The Leopard's Tale (2006); Hodder (ed.), Çatalhöyük Research Project volumes.

entries.label: The dead beneath the floor
entries.hint: The people of Çatalhöyük buried most of their dead under platforms and floors inside the houses, often reopening graves to remove the skull. Some skulls were plastered and even painted and then circulated before being reburied. The practice parallels the plastered skulls of the Levant and ties the town to a wider Neolithic world of ancestors kept close.
entries.note: Ian Hodder, The Leopard's Tale (2006); Çatalhöyük Research Project burial reports.

entries.label: The death pit at Domuztepe
entries.hint: In a village of the Halaf culture, a pit more than three metres across was filled with the broken bones of at least 40 people, mixed with those of cattle and with broken pottery, then capped with ash and marked with posts. It looks like a staged event with large-scale feasting, possibly including cannibalism; the animals and the humans were treated in distinct ways.
entries.note: Elizabeth Carter, Sarah Campbell and colleagues, Domuztepe excavation reports; Kansa and Campbell in Behaviour Behind Bones (2004); Anthropozoologica 44 (2009).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Carved pillars, the oldest life-size statue, painted walls and a seated figure between leopards

entries.label: The carved pillars of Göbekli Tepe
entries.hint: The T-pillars are stylised human figures: the best-preserved show arms carved along their sides, hands meeting over a belt and a fox-pelt loincloth. Their heads are abstract and faceless. Animals — foxes, boars, snakes, scorpions, vultures — crawl on their shafts in low relief. It is the earliest large-scale figurative sculpture known.
entries.note: Klaus Schmidt 2012; the Göbekli Tepe excavation reports of the German Archaeological Institute.

entries.label: The Urfa Man
entries.hint: A life-size limestone statue of a standing man with inlaid obsidian eyes, a necklace with a V-shape pendant and hands over a phallus, found in 1993 at Yeni Mahalle in Şanlıurfa, is the oldest known life-size human statue. Its style matches the carvings at Göbekli Tepe, and Şanlıurfa's museum holds it.
entries.note: Şanlıurfa Archaeology and Mosaic Museum; Harald Hauptmann and Klaus Schmidt on the Urfa statue, dated on stylistic and contextual comparison with Göbekli Tepe.

entries.label: Wall paintings at Çatalhöyük
entries.hint: Red, black and cream paintings cover interior walls: vultures hovering over headless figures, hunters baiting a bull, handprints and geometric patterns of plaited designs. Mellaart thought some panels depicted scenes; later study treats many as pattern. The paintings were replastered and overpainted again and again as the house was lived in.
entries.note: James Mellaart, Çatal Hüyük (1967); Ian Hodder, Çatalhöyük Research Project volumes.

entries.label: The sound record — a pipe from Bilecik
entries.hint: Musical evidence from Neolithic Anatolia is almost absent in the published record. A bone pipe with finger holes found with burials at Bahçelievler near Bilecik was reported in the Turkish press as the region's earliest instrument, about 8,500 years old, and it awaits full publication. Göbekli Tepe's enclosures are thought to have carried sound well, but no instrument comes from them.
entries.note: Report in Hürriyet Daily News on the Bilecik pipe; unpublished as of 2026. Treat the date and identification as provisional.

entries.label: The seated woman of Çatalhöyük
entries.hint: A fired-clay figure of a seated, heavy-bodied woman flanked by two leopards, the head a modern restoration, was found in a grain bin in 1961 and now stands in Ankara. Mellaart saw a mother goddess. Hodder points out that most of the site's figurines were found in rubbish, not in shrines, and that animals dominate the assemblage.
entries.note: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara; James Mellaart 1967; Lynn Meskell and Ian Hodder, on figurines, in Çatalhöyük Research Project volumes.

entries.label: The painted pottery of Hacılar
entries.hint: The best potters of the Lakes District painted thin-walled bowls and jars in red on a cream slip with bold triangles, chevrons and lattices, and later added modelled faces. Hacılar ware is among the earliest decorated pottery in Anatolia and the figurines of the same villages include seated women, couples and young men.
entries.note: James Mellaart, Excavations at Hacılar (1970).

entries.label: The painted walls of Arslantepe
entries.hint: The temple and the palace of Arslantepe carried wall paintings of red and black geometric designs on white plaster, with stylised figures, and the palace continued the tradition of painted and relief-decorated walls. It is among the earliest painted architecture of a state-like power, applied with careful planning to the surfaces that visitors saw.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane (ed.), Arslantepe excavation volumes (1993–).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: A pillar read as a sky record and a wall painting read as a map — both contested

entries.label: Pillar 43 as a record of the sky
entries.hint: Pillar 43, the 'Vulture Stone', carries a scorpion, a bird and a headless figure, and was read by Martin Sweatman and Dimitrios Tsikritsis in 2017 as a star chart recording a comet strike around 10,950 BC. The excavators and most specialists regard that reading as unproven; the animal symbols may equally be read within the pillars' social symbolism.
entries.note: Martin Sweatman and Dimitrios Tsikritsis, Mediterranean Archaeology and Archaeometry 17.1 (2017); contra the Göbekli Tepe excavators (DAI).

entries.label: Is the Çatalhöyük 'map' a map?
entries.hint: A wall painting from a building at Çatalhöyük, dated to around 6600 BC, shows a rectilinear grid of boxes with a double-peaked form above it. Mellaart read it as a plan of the town beneath the eruption of Hasan Dağ — the earliest map. Stephanie Meece argued in 2006 that the grid is a geometric pattern and the 'volcano' a leopard-skin; the map claim is now generally set aside.
entries.note: James Mellaart, Anatolian Studies 13 (1963); Stephanie Meece, 'A bird's eye view — of a leopard's spots', Anatolian Studies 56 (2006).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Einkorn from the Karacadağ, managed sheep, cattle and the first dairy products

entries.label: Einkorn domesticated in the Karacadağ
entries.hint: DNA fingerprinting of wild and cultivated einkorn showed that the domesticated crop descends from wild populations on the Karacadağ volcanic mountain, just a short distance from Çayönü and Göbekli Tepe. The farming economy of Europe and the Near East is traced to a small and well-defined area at the foot of the Taurus.
entries.note: Manfred Heun et al., 'Site of Einkorn Wheat Domestication Identified by DNA Fingerprinting', Science 278 (1997).

entries.label: Managing sheep at Aşıklı
entries.hint: The animal bones of Aşıklı show hunters of wild herds gradually turning to controlling sheep, shifting from broad-spectrum hunting over about nine centuries. Dung layers show that the villagers penned their animals within the settlement itself. The change was gradual and local.
entries.note: Mary Stiner et al., 'A forager–herder trade-off, from broad-spectrum hunting to sheep management at Aşıklı Höyük, Turkey', PNAS 111 (2014).

entries.label: Farming and herding at Çatalhöyük
entries.hint: The people of the town grew wheat, barley and legumes on the Konya plain, kept sheep and goats, hunted wild cattle and horses for feasts and, from about 6500 BC, kept domesticated cattle. Marsh resources and wild plants filled the gaps. The mix changed with time; as the town grew, it moved further from its fields and relied more on herds.
entries.note: Çatalhöyük Research Project archaeobotany and zooarchaeology volumes (Hodder, ed.); Nerissa Russell and Louise Martin in the same series.

entries.label: Dairying in western Anatolia
entries.hint: Chemical analysis of fat residues in more than two thousand pottery vessels found the oldest direct evidence of milk use in the Near East and southeastern Europe in the seventh millennium BC, strongest in northwest Anatolia where cattle herding was most important. The study ties the dairy products to the cattle, not the sheep and goats.
entries.note: Richard Evershed et al., 'Earliest date for milk use in the Near East and southeastern Europe linked to cattle herding', Nature 455 (2008).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Native copper, lime terrazzo, the first pottery, obsidian blades and the arsenical copper of Arslantepe

entries.label: Native copper at Çayönü
entries.hint: Beads, pins and an awl of native copper from Çayönü, hammered and annealed rather than smelted, are among the first worked metal objects in the world. The copper came from nearby ore outcrops at Ergani. Metal remained a decorative curiosity; smelting would not appear for several thousand years.
entries.note: Çayönü excavation reports (Braidwood, Çambel, Özdoğan); Ünsal Yalçın on the Çayönü copper in Anatolian metallurgy studies.

entries.label: Terrazzo and lime plaster
entries.hint: Çayönü's 'terrazzo building' had floors of lime mortar studded with polished stones and pebbles, a hard, waterproof surface. Making it meant burning limestone to produce lime, an early use of controlled fire for a building material, and lime plaster was also used on walls at Çatalhöyük.
entries.note: Çayönü excavation reports (Özdoğan and Erim-Özdoğan).

entries.label: Obsidian blades and mirrors
entries.hint: Cappadocian knappers produced long, regular blades from conical 'naviform' cores. Çatalhöyük added polished obsidian mirrors in burials, a sophisticated use of the volcanic glass. The industry depended on volcanic sources a hundred kilometres from the Konya plain.
entries.note: Nur Balkan-Atlı and Didier Binder on Cappadocian obsidian exploitation, in Cauvin et al. (eds), L'obsidienne au Proche et Moyen Orient (1998); Mellaart 1967.

entries.label: Pottery comes to central Anatolia
entries.hint: The first pottery in the region shows up around 7000 BC in the early levels of Çatalhöyük, as dark, burnished, thick-walled bowls. It was added to an economy that had managed for a long time without it, and in the western part of the site it becomes abundant only from about 6000 BC.
entries.note: Ian Hodder (ed.), Çatalhöyük Research Project volumes; Mellaart 1967.

entries.label: Arsenical copper and the swords of Arslantepe
entries.hint: The workshops of Arslantepe produced arsenical copper, an alloy that is harder and easier to cast than pure copper, and used it in some of the earliest swords of the Near East, found with spearheads in the burnt palace. Metal was now an elite tool and a weapon, and the arsenic ores came from the Eastern Anatolian highlands.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane (ed.), Arslantepe volumes; metal analyses by A. Hauptmann, A. Palmieri and colleagues.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Cappadocian obsidian across the Near East, a shared ritual sphere, farmers leaving Anatolia and an Uruk enclave on the Euphrates

entries.label: The Pre-Pottery Neolithic interaction sphere
entries.hint: Plastered skulls, similar flint tools, imported obsidian, domesticated animals and a common repertoire of animal and human images recur from the Taurus foothills to the Levant and the Syrian steppe. The communities were different but their symbols travelled. Jacques Cauvin argued that a shared symbolic revolution preceded and drove farming.
entries.note: Jacques Cauvin, The Birth of the Gods and the Origins of Agriculture (2000); Klaus Schmidt 2012.

entries.label: Cappadocian obsidian across the Near East
entries.hint: Obsidian chemically matched to the Göllü Dağ and Nenezi Dağ volcanoes turns up at village sites across Anatolia, in the northern Levant and on Cyprus, hundreds of kilometres away. The distribution is a map of the earliest long-distance exchange networks, in which the stone moved by hand to hand and not by merchant.
entries.note: Marie-Claire Cauvin et al. (eds), L'obsidienne au Proche et Moyen Orient (1998); Briois, Gratuze and Guilaine, 'Les obsidiennes de Shillourokambos (Chypre)', Paléorient 23 (1997).

entries.label: Anatolian farmers leave for Europe
entries.hint: Ancient DNA from the Marmara farming villages and from central Anatolia shows the first European farmers descend directly from the Aegean and Anatolian Neolithic populations. Farming did not spread through ideas alone, since people moved. The first farmers of Anatolia were themselves a fairly low-diversity population at the start.
entries.note: Gülşah Kılınç et al., Current Biology 26 (2016); Mathieson et al., Nature 555 (2018); Hofmanová et al., PNAS 113 (2016).

entries.label: The Ubaid reaches Cilicia
entries.hint: Pottery in the Mesopotamian Ubaid tradition reaches the Cilician coast and the Euphrates valley during the fifth millennium BC. The Mersin region took up the pottery forms but built its own fortified settlement, and the finds show contact with northern Syria and Mesopotamia without any sign of a colony.
entries.note: Isabella Caneva, Mara Palumbi and Pasquino on the Ubaid impact at Mersin-Yumuktepe; Palumbi and Caneva (eds) 2019.

entries.label: An Uruk enclave at Hacınebi
entries.hint: On the Euphrates, a local Anatolian settlement with its own elite hosted an enclave of people with Uruk Mesopotamian pottery, bevelled-rim bowls and sealing practices, living in one part of the site beside the locals. Gil Stein's excavations found an exchange between equals, not a colony that dominated its host.
entries.note: Gil Stein et al., 'Uruk Colonies and Anatolian Communities: An Interim Report on the 1992–1993 Excavations at Hacınebi', American Journal of Archaeology 100 (1996); Stein, Rethinking World-Systems (1999).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The end of the Ice Age cold, the 8.2 ka cold snap, the end of the Konya villages and the Kura-Araxes advance

entries.label: The end of the Younger Dryas
entries.hint: The abrupt end of the cold Younger Dryas around 9600 BC brought warmer, wetter conditions and richer stands of wild cereals to the Taurus foothills. The first monumental buildings and the first villages appear at the same time, though cause and effect remain debated.
entries.note: Klaus Schmidt 2012 (radiocarbon dates of the earliest Göbekli Tepe levels); Younger Dryas termination as dated in the ice cores.

entries.label: The 8.2 ka event and the early villages
entries.hint: A cold and dry spell of roughly a century and a half around 6200 BC hit the eastern Mediterranean. Some Anatolian villages were abandoned or shrank, and others rode it out. Later work stresses the resilience of farming communities to this event as much as the disruption.
entries.note: Bernhard Weninger et al., Quaternary Research 66 (2006); Zachary Flohr et al., Quaternary Science Reviews 136 (2016).

entries.label: The Konya villages disperse
entries.hint: The East Mound of Çatalhöyük was abandoned around 6000 BC. The West Mound and other nearby sites are occupied after that in a pattern of smaller, scattered households, not one great town. Why it dispersed is debated: climate, the state of the land and social change have all been proposed.
entries.note: Ian Hodder (ed.), Çatalhöyük Research Project volumes, esp. the West Mound studies.

entries.label: The Kura-Araxes reach the Upper Euphrates
entries.hint: A material culture with handburnished black-and-red pottery and round-hearthed houses spreads from the South Caucasus across eastern Anatolia and into the Euphrates valley around 3000 BC, replacing the Late Chalcolithic of the Malatya plain and its palaces. The people were mainly herders and farmers.
entries.note: Marcella Frangipane (ed.) 2010; Mitchell Rothman (ed.), Uruk Mesopotamia and Its Neighbors (2001).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Women and men at Çatalhöyük, the health cost of farming, and migrants beside locals at Hacınebi

entries.label: Women and men at Çatalhöyük
entries.hint: Mellaart read the figurines as a cult of the mother goddess and an early matriarchy. The skeletons suggest otherwise: women and men were buried alike, ate a similar diet, and show no consistent difference in the grave goods. Whatever the town's gender order was, the evidence points to relative equality and no sign of a dominant sex.
entries.note: Ian Hodder, The Leopard's Tale (2006); Larsen et al., PNAS 116 (2019).

entries.label: The health cost of farming
entries.hint: The skeletons of Çatalhöyük bear the marks of crowded village life: tooth decay, infections and signs of anaemia rise over the town's history, as the population grows and diet changes. Early farming did not make people healthier or taller; the gains were in numbers and stored food.
entries.note: Clark Spencer Larsen et al., PNAS 116 (2019).

entries.label: Migrants beside locals at Hacınebi
entries.hint: At Hacınebi the Mesopotamian enclave and the Anatolian townspeople used different pottery, cooked different foods and kept their own food practices — different proportions of animals eaten. Identity was a matter of daily habit made visible in material, not written or declared.
entries.note: Gil Stein, Rethinking World-Systems (1999); Stein et al., American Journal of Archaeology 100 (1996).
